title: Headache and Fatigue
introduction: Headache (cephalgia) and fatigue are two of the most frequent, multi-system symptoms nurses assess across hospital and community settings[cite: 371, 386]. Distinguishing primary from secondary headaches and differentiating normal, pathophysiological, situational, and psychological fatigue enables nurses to conduct targeted COLDSPA assessments and deliver safe, individualized interventions[cite: 373, 379, 389, 392].
learningOutcomes: 1.1 Define headache (cephalgia), identify pain-sensitive cranial structures, and distinguish primary from secondary headaches[cite: 371, 372, 373].
1.2 Compare the pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, stages, and diagnostic evaluations of tension-type, cluster, and migraine headaches[cite: 373, 374, 375, 376, 377, 378].
1.3 Apply the COLDSPA mnemonic, Gordon's Functional Health Patterns, non-pharmacological interventions, and drug therapies in managing patients with headache[cite: 379, 380, 381, 382].
1.4 Define fatigue, distinguish it from weakness, and explain Bartley's four-stage mechanism of fatigue[cite: 342, 386, 387, 388].
1.5 Classify the four types of fatigue, conduct subjective and objective nursing assessments, and formulate targeted nursing interventions[cite: 342, 388, 389, 390, 391, 392, 393].

content.heading: Meaning, Pain-Sensitive Structures, and Classification of Headache
content.body: Headache (also called cephalgia) is an unpleasant sensation in the region of the cranial vault and the area below the orbits (eyes), spreading over the scalp and back to the occipital region (Jacobs & Geels, 1985)[cite: 371]. Not all cranial tissues are sensitive to pain; the pain-sensitive structures include the venous sinuses, the dura, cranial blood vessels, the three divisions of cranial nerve V (trigeminal), CN VII (facial), CN IX (glossopharyngeal), CN X (vagus), and the first three cervical nerves (Lewis et al., 2007)[cite: 372]. Headaches are classified into two broad categories: Primary headaches, which have no associated organic cause (tension-type, migraine, and cluster headaches), and Secondary headaches, which result from underlying organic causes such as brain tumours, aneurysms, or increased intracranial pressure[cite: 373].

content.heading: Tension-Type Headache (TTH) and Cluster Headache
content.body: Tension-type headache (TTH) is the most common primary headache, presenting as mild-to-moderate, bilateral pressing or tightening ('band-like') pain aggravated by activities and linked to emotional or physical stress[cite: 373, 374, 378]. The International Headache Society divides TTH into Episodic TTH (fewer than 15 headache-days per month) and Chronic TTH (15 or more headache-days per month, often causing greater disability, mild nausea, anxiety, depression, and medication overuse)[cite: 374, 375]. Empirical evidence links TTH to heightened central nervous system excitability from sustained pericranial myofascial input, pericranial myofascial tenderness (Bendtsen & Jensen, 2009), nitric oxide (NO) pathways, and elevated peripheral calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) in chronic TTH[cite: 374]. Patients may experience either photophobia or phonophobia, though not together, and electromyography (EMG) may show sustained contraction of neck, scalp, and facial muscles[cite: 375]. Cluster headaches are a rare vascular headache occurring in clusters of 1 to 8 attacks daily for 4 to 8 weeks before remitting for months to years[cite: 375]. They cause excruciating, strictly unilateral pain around one eye, orbit, temple, forehead, and cheek accompanied by tearing, nasal congestion/rhinitis, facial flushing or pallor, drooping eyelids, and restlessness, and are characteristically relieved by walking around[cite: 375, 376]. Pathophysiology involves the trigeminal nerve, intracranial vessels, sympathetic and pain modulation systems, the hypothalamus (explaining circadian rhythmicity), genetic predisposition, smoking, and alcohol[cite: 376].

content.heading: Migraine Headache: Pathophysiology, Stages, and Diagnosis
content.body: Migraine is a recurring, familial headache marked by severe unilateral or bilateral throbbing pain (commonly supra-orbital, retro-orbital, or fronto-temporal) with neurologic and autonomic symptoms, characteristically relieved by lying down[cite: 376]. Three pathophysiologic theories are proposed: sudden vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation altering blood flow, muscular tension in the head, and biochemical alterations in the serotonin pathway[cite: 376]. Classic migraine progresses through four stages: (1) Prodromal Phase—depression, irritability, food cravings, anorexia, and fluid balance shifts; (2) Aura Phase—visual disturbances (light flashes, bright spots on one side of the visual field), warmth, mild confusion, slight extremity weakness, drowsiness, and dizziness driven by spreading depression and diminished cerebral blood flow (oligemia) advancing from the occipital to frontal lobe at 2–3 mm/min (taking medication here can prevent a full attack); (3) Headache Phase—incapacitating throbbing pain synchronized with the pulse lasting 4–72 hours during which patients 'hibernate' from light, sound, odours, and people; and (4) Recovery (Postdromal) Phase—gradual symptom resolution accompanied by neck/scalp muscle contraction, localized tenderness, exhaustion, mood shifts, and prolonged sleep[cite: 377]. Diagnosis relies primarily on history; head CT or MRI is reserved for abnormal neurological exam findings[cite: 378].

content.heading: Nursing Assessment, Interventions, and Pharmacotherapy for Headache
content.body: Accurate nursing history uses Weber and Kelly's (2007) COLDSPA mnemonic—Characteristic, Onset, Location, Duration, Severity, Pattern, and Alleviating/Associated factors—alongside a patient headache diary and Marjory Gordon's Functional Health Patterns (health perception, nutrition, activity, sleep-rest, cognitive-perceptual, self-concept, coping-stress, and role-relationship)[cite: 379, 380]. Common nursing diagnoses include acute pain, altered comfort, impaired visual sensory perception (photophobia), altered self-concept, knowledge deficit, and ineffective coping[cite: 380]. Non-pharmacologic nursing interventions include identifying lifestyle stressors and dietary triggers (amines such as cheese and chocolate, nitrites in hot dogs, vinegar, onions, MSG, caffeine, red wine/alcohol, nicotine, and aspartame), teaching relaxation techniques (meditation, self-hypnosis, imagery), applying massage and moist heat to the head and neck for TTH, and providing a quiet, dimly lit environment for migraine[cite: 381]. Pharmacotherapy varies by type: TTH responds to non-opioid analgesics (aspirin, acetaminophen) alone or combined with a sedative, muscle relaxant, tranquilizer, or codeine[cite: 382]; cluster headaches use prophylactic agents such as verapamil, lithium, ergotamine tartrate, and NSAIDs[cite: 382]; mild-to-moderate migraines respond to non-opioids, whereas moderate-to-severe migraines use triptans as first-line drugs (sumatriptan, naratriptan, rizatriptan, eletriptan, almotriptan) to act on serotonin receptors, reduce neurogenic vascular inflammation, and cause vasoconstriction[cite: 382]. Preventive migraine drugs include beta-blockers (propranolol, atenolol), tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), SSRIs (fluoxetine), calcium channel blockers (verapamil), and clonidine[cite: 382].

content.heading: Meaning, Mechanism, and Four Types of Fatigue
content.body: Fatigue is a feeling of tiredness, exhaustion, or need to rest due to lack of energy or strength, with primary causes including overwork, impaired sleep pattern, psychological disturbance, and lack of exercise[cite: 342, 386]. Fatigue may also be secondary to illness or treatments like chemotherapy, and it is not synonymous with weakness: weakness denotes a neuromuscular problem, whereas fatigue is a systemic response affecting all body systems[cite: 342, 387]. Bartley (cited in Jacobs & Geels, 1985) outlined four sequential processes in the mechanism of fatigue: (1) Cellular Impairment—depletion of oxygen, ATP, and glycogen with accumulation of lactic acid and pyruvate, reducing muscle contraction efficiency and delaying recovery; (2) Systemic Disorganization—loss of coordinated organ-system integration (which can also be triggered directly by psychological anxiety, producing palpitations and diarrhoea); (3) Discomfort—subjective muscular, sensory, or cognitive discomfort compelling cessation of activity; and (4) Decrease in Activity—objective drop in productivity, physical output, and mental function[cite: 342, 387, 388]. Fatigue is categorized into four types: Normal fatigue (expected after exertion, hectic schedules, or poor sleep; resolves quickly with rest and moderate lifestyle changes), Pathophysiological fatigue (symptom/outcome of acute febrile infections or chronic diseases like COPD, heart failure, and nutritional disorders; cannot be resolved by rest alone), Situational fatigue (a variant of normal fatigue occurring when coping mechanisms are depleted during crises such as career change, bereavement, or marriage crises, causing helplessness and anxiety), and Psychological fatigue (secondary to depression or prolonged anxiety, marked by loss of interest, slowed psychomotor responses, and prolonged recovery)[cite: 342, 388, 389].

content.heading: Clinical Manifestations, Assessment, and Nursing Interventions for Fatigue
content.body: Common manifestations of fatigue depend on the underlying type and include rapid heart and respiratory rates (anxiety), inability to complete work, weariness, flat affect, weight changes (nutritional disorders), and dyspnoea (heart or lung disease)[cite: 342, 390]. Subjective nursing assessment explores activity and role changes, sleep-rest hours, fatigue patterns (normal improves with rest; prolonged suggests psychological causes), associated symptoms (fever/malaise for acute illness; weight loss for nutritional disorders, hypothyroidism, or neoplasm; dyspnoea for CHF, anaemia, or COPD), stressors, diet, medications (antihypertensives, tranquilizers, hypnotics, antidepressants), family history, and COLDSPA symptom exploration[cite: 390, 391]. Objective head-to-toe examination observes general appearance before formal interaction (elevated stiff shoulders or fidgeting suggest anxiety; apathy, crying, or poor eye contact suggest depression; a mask-like face suggests Parkinson's disease; staring watchfulness suggests metabolic disorders or anxiety), vital signs (tachycardia, tachypnoea), integument (pallor/cyanosis in anaemia, heart failure, or lung disease; jaundice in liver disease; nail clubbing in poor oxygenation), and full systemic checks[cite: 391, 392]. Nursing interventions encompass physical care, monitoring medical regimens, counselling, teaching, and referral, anchored in a trusting nurse-patient relationship[cite: 342, 392]. General measures include exercise, adequate sleep, stress reduction, and motivation; normal fatigue focuses on rest and ADL scheduling, pathophysiological fatigue treats the underlying disease while monitoring therapy response collaboratively, and situational fatigue guides crisis problem-solving in three steps: (1) understand the patient's perception of the event, (2) identify available supports, and (3) assess previous coping methods[cite: 392, 393].

inTextQuestions.question: A patient wakes from a nap with excruciating unilateral pain around one eye, drooping eyelids, and nasal stuffiness that improves only when walking around. Which type of primary headache is suspected?
What distinguishes Episodic Tension-Type Headache from Chronic Tension-Type Headache according to the International Headache Society?
inTextQuestions.answer: Episodic TTH occurs on fewer than 15 headache-days per month, whereas Chronic TTH occurs on 15 or more headache-days per month and is more likely to cause disability and medication overuse[cite: 374].

inTextQuestions.question: Why is fatigue not clinically synonymous with weakness?
inTextQuestions.answer: Weakness specifically denotes a neuromuscular problem, whereas fatigue is a net systemic response to cellular impairment and systemic or psychological disorganization affecting all body systems[cite: 342, 387, 388].

inTextQuestions.question: During a head-to-toe assessment of a fatigued patient, what underlying conditions might nail clubbing, jaundice, or a mask-like facial expression suggest?
inTextQuestions.answer: Nail clubbing suggests poor oxygenation status, jaundice suggests liver disease, and an expressionless, mask-like face is common in Parkinson's disease[cite: 391, 392].

saqs.question: Define headache (cephalgia), list the pain-sensitive structures of the cranium, and differentiate primary from secondary headaches.
saqs.answer: Headache (cephalgia) is an unpleasant sensation in the cranial vault and below the orbits, spreading over the scalp to the occipital region[cite: 371]. Pain-sensitive cranial structures are the venous sinuses, dura, cranial blood vessels, three divisions of CN V (trigeminal), CN VII (facial), CN IX (glossopharyngeal), CN X (vagus), and the first three cervical nerves[cite: 372]. Primary headaches (tension-type, migraine, cluster) have no associated organic cause, whereas secondary headaches stem from organic causes like brain tumour, aneurysm, or increased intracranial pressure[cite: 373].

saqs.question: Outline the four phases of a classic migraine headache and state why triptans are first-line drugs for moderate-to-severe migraines.
saqs.answer: The four phases are: (1) Prodromal Phase (irritability, depression, food cravings, anorexia, fluid shifts), (2) Aura Phase (visual flashes/spots, warmth, confusion, weakness from spreading oligemia moving occipital-to-frontal at 2–3 mm/min), (3) Headache Phase (4–72 hours of incapacitating throbbing pain with hibernation from stimuli), and (4) Recovery/Postdromal Phase (gradual cessation, neck/scalp tenderness, exhaustion, prolonged sleep)[cite: 377]. Triptans (e.g., sumatriptan) are first-line because they selectively target serotonin receptors, reduce neurogenic inflammation of cerebral blood vessels, and induce vasoconstriction[cite: 382].

saqs.question: Expand the COLDSPA mnemonic used in nursing assessment of headache and fatigue, and list five dietary or lifestyle triggers to avoid in headache care.
saqs.answer: COLDSPA stands for Characteristic, Onset, Location, Duration, Severity, Pattern, and Alleviating/Associated factors[cite: 379, 384]. Five triggers to identify and avoid include amine-containing foods (cheese, chocolate), nitrites (hot dogs), monosodium glutamate (MSG), caffeine, and alcohol (red wine) or nicotine[cite: 381].

saqs.question: Explain Bartley's four-stage mechanism of fatigue and differentiate the four clinical types of fatigue.
saqs.answer: Bartley's four stages are: (1) Cellular Impairment (depletion of oxygen, ATP, and glycogen with lactic acid/pyruvate buildup), (2) Systemic Disorganization (uncoordinated organ systems, also inducible by anxiety), (3) Discomfort (subjective sensory/muscular ache halting activity), and (4) Decrease in Activity (objective drop in productivity and mental/physical output)[cite: 387, 388]. The four types are Normal fatigue (resolves with rest), Pathophysiological fatigue (caused by acute/chronic disease; does not resolve with rest alone), Situational fatigue (depleted coping in life crises), and Psychological fatigue (secondary to depression or prolonged anxiety)[cite: 389].

saqs.question: List the five core domains of nursing intervention for fatigue and state the three problem-solving steps required for managing situational fatigue.
saqs.answer: The five nursing intervention domains are physical care, monitoring medical regimen, counselling, teaching, and referral—built on a trusting nurse-patient relationship[cite: 342, 392]. For situational fatigue, the nurse guides problem solving in three steps: (1) understand the patient's perception of the crisis event, (2) identify available supports, and (3) assess the patient's previous methods of coping[cite: 392, 393].
